questions.question: What is Spring Boot and why was it created?
questions.title: What is Spring Boot?
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot is a project built on Spring Framework that makes it easier to create stand-alone Spring applications. It was created to remove repeated setup by providing managed starter dependencies, conditional auto-configuration, external settings, and executable applications with embedded-server support.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Spring Boot builds on Spring Framework; it does not replace Spring.
Starters provide a convenient set of related, version-managed dependencies.
Auto-configuration supplies common beans when its classpath, property, and bean conditions match.
Application properties and environment variables keep settings outside the Java code.
An embedded server and an executable JAR make many web applications easy to run with `java -jar`.
Boot provides defaults, but application configuration can replace or disable them.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Spring Boot is a project built on top of Spring Framework. The application still uses Spring's container, dependency injection, configuration, transactions, and web framework. Boot makes those parts quicker to assemble by supplying sensible defaults for common application types.

The main tools are starters and auto-configuration. A starter such as `spring-boot-starter-web` brings the related libraries that a typical web application needs. Boot then looks at the classes, properties, and beans available to the application and applies matching auto-configuration. For example, when Spring MVC and an embedded servlet container are present, Boot can create the usual web infrastructure and start the server.

A small application can therefore begin with one dependency and a main class that calls `SpringApplication.run`. The developer adds controllers and business code instead of first wiring the server, JSON converter, and MVC setup by hand. Settings such as a port or database URL can come from property files, environment variables, or command-line arguments, so the same application can run in different environments.

These features are defaults, not fixed rules. Many auto-configurations use missing-bean conditions, so a bean supplied by the application can make Boot back off. A configuration can also be excluded when it is not wanted.

Spring Boot was created to make common Spring setup repeatable and to help applications start and run with less manual configuration. It does not remove the need to understand Spring or design the application well; it removes much of the setup work around those decisions.

sections.title: How Spring Boot turns dependencies into a running application
sections.content:
**The problem Boot solves**

A Spring application needs an `ApplicationContext`, application beans, third-party libraries, configuration values, and a way to start. A web application also needs HTTP infrastructure and a server. These parts existed before Spring Boot, but each project had to choose compatible versions and repeat much of the same setup.

**What Boot adds**

A starter is a dependency descriptor for one kind of application. The web starter, for example, gives the project a supported web stack without asking the developer to select each library and version separately. Auto-configuration then checks conditions such as “is this class present?”, “is this property enabled?”, and “has the application already defined this bean?” Matching configuration contributes the usual beans.

This is why adding a dependency can change startup behaviour. The dependency puts capabilities on the classpath; auto-configuration notices those capabilities. The two features work well together, but they are not the same thing: a starter selects libraries, while auto-configuration creates configuration from the environment it sees.

**How an application keeps control**

Boot's configuration is conditional. If the application defines a bean that an auto-configuration only provides when missing, the application's bean wins. Properties can tune many defaults, and unwanted auto-configurations can be excluded. Boot therefore starts with conventions but keeps Spring's normal configuration model available.

Production-oriented features such as external configuration, logging integration, health information, and executable packaging complete the application experience. They make deployment and operation more consistent; they do not make every generated application production-ready by themselves. Security, data design, testing, and capacity planning still belong to the application team.

sections.title: From one starter to a running web application
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
  D["spring-boot-starter-web"] --> C["Supported libraries on the classpath"]
  C --> A["Auto-configuration checks conditions"]
  P["Properties and environment"] --> A
  U["Application-defined beans"] --> A
  A --> X["ApplicationContext with matching beans"]
  X --> S["Embedded server starts the web application"]
```

questions.question: What does @SpringBootApplication do?
questions.title: @SpringBootApplication annotation explained
questions.direct_answer: `@SpringBootApplication` marks the main configuration class and combines `@SpringBootConfiguration`, `@EnableAutoConfiguration`, and `@ComponentScan`. Together they identify Boot configuration, enable conditional auto-configuration, and scan the class's package and its subpackages for application components.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `@SpringBootConfiguration` identifies the application's main Boot configuration class and is a specialized form of `@Configuration`.
`@EnableAutoConfiguration` imports auto-configuration whose conditions match the application.
`@ComponentScan` finds components in the annotated class's package and its subpackages.
Place the application class in a root package so controllers, services, and repositories sit below it.
Use `exclude` or `excludeName` when a specific auto-configuration must not apply.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`@SpringBootApplication` is a convenience annotation for the main configuration class of a Spring Boot application. It combines `@SpringBootConfiguration`, `@EnableAutoConfiguration`, and `@ComponentScan`, so one annotation starts three related parts of application setup.

`@SpringBootConfiguration` identifies the class as Boot's main configuration source. It is a specialized `@Configuration`, so the class can also declare `@Bean` methods. `@EnableAutoConfiguration` asks Boot to import configuration whose conditions match the application. For example, web auto-configuration becomes relevant when the web classes are present, and a missing-bean condition lets application configuration replace a default.

`@ComponentScan` discovers classes such as controllers, services, repositories, and other components. With no custom scan package, scanning begins in the package that contains the annotated class and continues through its subpackages. If `BillingApplication` is in `com.example.billing`, a controller in `com.example.billing.web` is found, but one in the separate package `com.example.shared` is not found by that default scan.

That package rule is why the main class normally sits near the top of the application's package tree. It gives the application a clear scan boundary without listing every feature package. If the layout cannot follow that rule, scanning can be configured explicitly, although a broad scan should not hide a confusing package structure.

The annotation is convenient rather than magical. Its `exclude` and `excludeName` attributes can disable a specific auto-configuration. It does not scan every class on the classpath, and it does not turn ordinary classes into beans unless a configuration mechanism registers them.

sections.title: What each part contributes
sections.content:
**The configuration source**

Spring needs configuration that tells its container which beans belong in the application. `@SpringBootConfiguration` marks the main Boot configuration class and is itself annotated with `@Configuration`. The class passed to `SpringApplication.run` is normally this class.

**The auto-configuration switch**

`@EnableAutoConfiguration` imports Boot's auto-configuration candidates. Those candidates contain conditions. A servlet web configuration may require servlet classes, a data configuration may require a particular API, and many bean definitions apply only if the application has not supplied an equivalent bean. This is how Boot adds defaults without treating every project as identical.

**The application scan**

`@ComponentScan` looks for component stereotypes from its base package. The package of the application class becomes the default scan root, so package placement affects which controllers and services exist in the context. The auto-configuration package also uses that location as a default for features such as entity scanning.

The three concerns can be declared separately, but most applications do not gain anything from doing so. Keep one clear application class, place it above the feature packages, and use a targeted exclusion or explicit scan package only when the project has a real reason. Multiple application annotations or an unnecessarily broad scan make the context harder to understand and test.

sections.title: The three jobs of @SpringBootApplication
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A["@SpringBootApplication"] --> C["@SpringBootConfiguration
main configuration source"] A --> E["@EnableAutoConfiguration
conditional Boot defaults"] A --> S["@ComponentScan
application components below this package"] C --> X["ApplicationContext"] E --> X S --> X ```

questions.question: What is the Spring Boot parent POM and why do projects use it?
questions.title: Spring Boot parent POM and dependency management
questions.direct_answer: `spring-boot-starter-parent` is a Maven parent POM that gives a Spring Boot project dependency management and useful build defaults. Projects use it to omit versions for supported dependencies, receive compatible version choices, and use preconfigured plugin settings, including the executable-JAR repackage execution.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `spring-boot-starter-parent` is a Maven parent, not a library added to the runtime classpath.
It inherits dependency management from `spring-boot-dependencies`, so supported dependency versions can usually be omitted.
It also supplies Maven build defaults and plugin configuration.
The parent does not add web, data, or test libraries by itself; starters are separate dependencies.
A project that already has another parent can import the Spring Boot dependency BOM instead, but the BOM does not provide the parent's plugin management.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`spring-boot-starter-parent` is a parent POM for Maven-based Spring Boot projects. A child project declares it in the `<parent>` section of `pom.xml`. The parent supplies dependency management and useful build defaults; it is not an application library and it does not add web or database dependencies by itself.

Dependency management is the main benefit. Spring Boot publishes a tested set of versions for Spring libraries and many common third-party libraries. When a project declares `spring-boot-starter-web`, for example, it normally leaves out the version and receives the version managed by the selected Boot release. This reduces accidental combinations such as one Spring module from one release line and another module from a different line.

The parent also provides Maven defaults and plugin configuration. For executable packaging, it preconfigures the `repackage` execution; the project still declares the `spring-boot-maven-plugin`. A normal `mvn package` can then create the executable Boot archive.

For a Spring Boot 3.3.1 project, the parent version fixes the dependency-management baseline at 3.3.1. A project can override a managed version, but that changes part of a tested set and should be done for a clear compatibility or security reason, followed by testing.

The parent is optional. A company project may already have a corporate parent POM. In that case it can import the `spring-boot-dependencies` BOM in `<dependencyManagement>`. That keeps Boot's dependency versions but not all of the parent's plugin management and build defaults. Starters, the parent, and the BOM solve different problems and should not be treated as the same thing.

sections.title: How Maven receives Spring Boot's version choices
sections.content:
**A parent is part of the build model**

Maven combines a project's POM with its parent before it resolves dependencies and plugins. `spring-boot-starter-parent` inherits from `spring-boot-dependencies`, which contains the managed version set for a Boot release. Dependency management supplies a version when the child declares a matching dependency without one. It does not add that dependency automatically.

This distinction matters. The parent can manage the version of Jackson, but Jackson reaches the application only when the project or one of its dependencies requests it. A starter is a convenient request for a related dependency set; the parent keeps the versions of that set aligned.

**The build side**

The parent also configures common Maven properties and plugins. One important Boot-specific default is the `repackage` execution. Declaring the Spring Boot Maven plugin is enough for the parent's execution to participate in the package lifecycle. Without the parent, the project may need to configure that execution itself.

**When another parent already exists**

Maven gives a project one direct parent. If an organization requires its own parent, import `spring-boot-dependencies` as a BOM under `<dependencyManagement>`. The project retains its corporate parent and receives Boot's dependency versions, but it must manage the build-plugin setup that the Boot parent would otherwise provide.

A managed version is a tested default, not a ban on change. Override one only after checking why it is needed, whether Boot documents a property for it, and whether the resulting application still passes its tests.

sections.title: Parent POM, dependency BOM, and starter
sections.content:
| Item | Where it is declared | What it provides | What it does not do |
|---|---|---|---|
| `spring-boot-starter-parent` | `<parent>` | Managed dependency versions plus Maven defaults and plugin configuration | Add web or data libraries by itself |
| `spring-boot-dependencies` | Imported under `<dependencyManagement>` | Managed dependency versions | Provide all parent plugin defaults |
| A Boot starter | `<dependencies>` | A related dependency set for one capability | Act as the Maven parent |

sections.title: Spring Boot 3.3.1 parent with a versionless starter
sections.content:
```xml
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <parent>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
        <version>3.3.1</version>
        <relativePath/>
    </parent>

    <groupId>com.example</groupId>
    <artifactId>catalog-service</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0</version>

    <properties>
        <java.version>17</java.version>
    </properties>

    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

    <build>
        <plugins>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>
```

The web starter has no version because the parent manages it. The plugin is still declared; the parent supplies the repackage execution used during `mvn package`.

questions.question: What is the Spring Initializr and how do you use it?
questions.title: Spring Initializr — project bootstrapping
questions.direct_answer: Spring Initializr is a project-generation service for JVM applications, commonly used through `start.spring.io` or an IDE. You choose the build system, language, Spring Boot version, project coordinates, Java version, packaging, and dependencies; it returns a ready-to-import project skeleton.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Spring Initializr generates a JVM project skeleton from a set of selected options.
Choose Maven or Gradle, Java, Boot 3.3.1, JAR packaging, Java 17, project coordinates, and the needed dependencies.
The generated project normally includes the build file, wrapper, source folders, main application class, test class, and configuration file.
Import the project, inspect the generated build, run its tests, and start the application before adding business code.
Initializr is a starting tool, not part of the application's runtime and not a complete production architecture.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Spring Initializr is a service that generates the starting structure of a JVM project. Spring developers usually meet it through `start.spring.io`, and many IDE project wizards use the same kind of Initializr service. It saves time by producing a consistent build file and source layout from a small set of choices.

To create a Spring Boot 3.3.1 Java project, I would choose Maven or Gradle, Java as the language, JAR packaging, Java 17, and the group and artifact names. I would then select only the dependencies needed for the first feature, such as Spring Web for a REST service and Validation for request validation. Initializr checks its metadata and compatibility rules and generates a project archive.

After extracting the archive, I would import the generated Maven or Gradle project into the IDE. The project normally contains a build file, the build wrapper, standard source and test directories, a main class with `@SpringBootApplication`, a basic context test, and an application configuration file. I would read the build file rather than treating generated dependencies as a black box.

The first check is to run the test and start the empty application. That confirms the chosen Java version, Boot version, dependency download, and project setup before business code makes failures harder to separate. Then I can add the first controller or service and its tests.

Initializr does not generate the domain model, security policy, database design, deployment plan, or production checks. It creates a clean starting point. The team still owns every dependency choice and every design decision that follows.

sections.title: What Spring Initializr generates and what it leaves to you
sections.content:
**Inputs become project metadata**

An Initializr service publishes the project types, languages, Java and platform versions, packaging choices, and dependencies it supports. A browser, IDE, or command-line client sends the selected values to that service. The generator uses them to build project assets instead of copying one fixed template for every request.

For a Maven project, the important output is `pom.xml`; for Gradle it is a Gradle build. The build file records the chosen Boot version, coordinates, Java target, and dependencies. The archive also gives the project the standard source layout, wrapper scripts, an application class, a small context test, and a properties or YAML file. Exact files can vary with the selected project type and service version.

**A safe first run**

Open the generated build and make sure every dependency has a reason. Run the wrapper's test command, then run the application. If the empty context cannot start, fix the Java version, repository, proxy, or dependency issue before adding application features. This small check gives a known-good baseline.

**A generator, not an architect**

The generated project knows which libraries were requested, but it does not know the business rules. It cannot decide service boundaries, data ownership, authorization, API contracts, or operational limits. It also does not make a dependency safe merely because it appeared in the generated build. Review and update the project like any other source code.

Java version, packaging, and dependencies"] --> G["Initializr generates project assets"] G --> F["Build file, wrapper, source tree,
main class, test, and configuration"] F --> I["Import and inspect the build"] I --> T["Run tests and start the empty application"] T --> B["Add the first feature and its tests"] ```

questions.question: What is the difference between a fat JAR and a regular JAR in Spring Boot?
questions.title: Spring Boot fat JAR (uber JAR)
questions.direct_answer: A regular JAR is an archive that normally contains an application's own classes and resources, while its dependencies stay elsewhere on the runtime classpath. A Spring Boot executable fat JAR is an archive that also carries dependency JARs and Boot loader classes, so the application can usually start with `java -jar app.jar`.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A regular application JAR usually needs dependency JARs supplied separately on the classpath.
A Boot executable JAR contains application classes, dependency JARs, and Boot loader classes.
Application classes are stored under `BOOT-INF/classes`; dependencies are stored as nested JARs under `BOOT-INF/lib`.
The Spring Boot Maven plugin's `repackage` goal turns the ordinary archive into an executable Boot archive.
A Boot fat JAR is not the same as flattening all dependency classes into one shaded directory.
An embedded server is included only when the application's dependencies include one.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A regular JAR normally packages an application's compiled classes, resources, and manifest. Libraries that the application depends on are separate JARs and must be placed on the runtime classpath by a launch script, application server, or another tool.

A Spring Boot executable fat JAR packages the application and its runtime dependencies together. The application's classes and resources go under `BOOT-INF/classes`, dependency JARs go under `BOOT-INF/lib`, and Spring Boot loader classes know how to load that nested layout. The manifest points the Java launcher to the Boot launcher, which then starts the application's configured main class.

For example, the Spring Boot Maven plugin can repackage `catalog-service.jar`. The deployed machine receives that one application archive and can run `java -jar catalog-service.jar` with Java 17. If it is a servlet web application using the web starter, its embedded server dependency is inside the archive as well, so no separate Tomcat installation is required.

The term “fat JAR” is convenient, but Boot's archive is not simply every dependency unpacked into one flat directory. It keeps dependency JARs nested. That preserves their boundaries and lets Boot's loader handle them. A shaded or traditional uber JAR often merges dependency contents, which is a different packaging technique.

The trade-off is size and duplication across services: each executable archive can carry many of the same libraries. The benefit is a self-contained and repeatable application artifact. Layered archive metadata can help container-image builds separate dependencies from frequently changing application code, but it does not change the basic `BOOT-INF` executable layout.

sections.title: How the executable archive is built and launched
sections.content:
**Two different runtime arrangements**

Java can load application classes from one JAR and libraries from many other JARs listed on the classpath. That is the usual regular-JAR arrangement. Deployment must keep the main archive, its dependency directory, and the launch command in agreement.

Spring Boot's build plugin first lets the normal build create an archive, then the `repackage` goal creates an executable layout. Application content is placed in `BOOT-INF/classes`, runtime libraries remain as nested JARs in `BOOT-INF/lib`, and loader classes are added. Manifest entries identify the launcher and the application's start class.

When `java -jar` opens the archive, the Boot launcher builds the class-loading view for the application content and nested libraries, then invokes the application main class. The archive can therefore move as one unit as long as the target has a compatible Java runtime and any external services or configuration the application needs.

**What “self-contained” does not mean**

The archive does not contain the Java runtime, database, message broker, secrets, or every operating-system dependency. It contains the application's Java runtime classpath. A non-web Boot application may have no server at all; the embedded server appears because a web stack requested it.

Layered JAR metadata groups content such as stable dependencies and changing application classes for container tools. It improves layer reuse when images are rebuilt, but it is still the same executable archive model.

sections.title: Regular JAR versus Spring Boot executable JAR
sections.content:
| Concern | Regular application JAR | Spring Boot executable fat JAR |
|---|---|---|
| Application classes | Usually at the archive root | `BOOT-INF/classes` |
| Dependency libraries | Supplied as separate classpath entries | Nested JARs under `BOOT-INF/lib` |
| Launch | Often needs an explicit classpath and main class | Usually `java -jar app.jar` |
| Launcher | Application main class or external tooling | Boot launcher delegates to the application start class |
| Typical size | Smaller application archive | Larger because runtime dependencies are included |

sections.title: Inspect and run the packaged archive
sections.content:
```shell
$ jar tf target/catalog-service.jar | grep '^BOOT-INF/' | head
BOOT-INF/classes/
BOOT-INF/classes/com/example/catalog/CatalogApplication.class
BOOT-INF/lib/
BOOT-INF/lib/spring-boot-3.3.1.jar

$ java -jar target/catalog-service.jar
```

The listing shows application classes and nested dependency JARs in different directories. Exact dependency filenames depend on the project's managed dependency set.

questions.question: What happens when you run SpringApplication.run()?
questions.title: Spring Boot application startup sequence
questions.direct_answer: `SpringApplication.run()` prepares the application environment, creates the right `ApplicationContext`, loads the application's configuration and beans, refreshes the context, starts an embedded web server when the application is web-based, runs `ApplicationRunner` and `CommandLineRunner` beans, and returns the ready context or reports a startup failure.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Boot prepares an `Environment` from configuration sources, profiles, and command-line arguments.
It chooses and creates an `ApplicationContext` that matches the application type.
The primary source is loaded, component scanning and auto-configuration contribute bean definitions, and the context is refreshed.
During refresh, singleton beans are created and a web application starts its embedded server.
After refresh, `ApplicationRunner` and `CommandLineRunner` beans run before the ready event.
The method returns a `ConfigurableApplicationContext`; an exception produces startup failure handling instead of a ready application.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`SpringApplication.run(MyApplication.class, args)` is the call that bootstraps a Spring Boot application. It creates and refreshes Spring's application context, but several setup stages happen around that refresh. The method finally returns a `ConfigurableApplicationContext` when startup succeeds.

First, Boot prepares the application environment. It combines property sources such as application configuration, environment variables, system properties, and command-line arguments, then determines active profiles. Some early application events are published while this setup is happening, even before an application context exists.

Next, Boot selects an application-context type from the classpath and application settings. A servlet web application gets a servlet web server context; a reactive application gets the reactive form; a non-web application uses a regular context. Boot applies context initializers and loads the main application class as a configuration source.

When the context is refreshed, Spring processes configuration, component scanning, and auto-configuration, registers bean definitions, invokes container extension points, and creates non-lazy singleton beans. In a web application, the embedded server is created and started as part of this context lifecycle. A constructor error, missing dependency, invalid configuration, or port conflict can stop startup here.

After refresh, Boot publishes its started and liveness signals, then calls ordered `ApplicationRunner` and `CommandLineRunner` beans. When those runners finish, Boot publishes the ready event and readiness signal. Runners are useful for startup work that needs the complete context, but long or fragile work delays readiness.

If startup throws an exception, Boot reports failure and publishes an application-failed event when possible. The exact internal classes can change between releases, so the useful model is environment, context, bean refresh and server, runners, then ready—not memorizing every private method.

sections.title: Spring Boot startup from main method to readiness
sections.content:
**Before the context exists**

The static `run` method creates a `SpringApplication` for the supplied primary source and starts its lifecycle. Listeners and initializers are prepared, startup begins, and Boot builds the `Environment`. Command-line arguments are available as a property source. Early events such as the starting and environment-prepared events happen before beans can receive them, because the context does not yet exist.

**Build and refresh the context**

Boot works out whether the application is servlet, reactive, or non-web and creates a matching context. Initializers run before bean definitions are loaded. The primary source is then loaded. In a typical application, its annotations lead to component scanning and auto-configuration imports.

Refresh is the central Spring step. Bean definitions are prepared, post-processors can modify the container, and non-lazy singleton beans are instantiated. Dependency cycles, constructor failures, missing configuration, and validation errors usually surface here. A web-server application also creates and starts its server while the context is being refreshed, after which a web-server-initialized event can be sent.

**Started is not yet ready**

After refresh, Boot publishes `ApplicationStartedEvent` and marks liveness correct. It then invokes `ApplicationRunner` and `CommandLineRunner` beans in their configured order. Only after the runners finish does `ApplicationReadyEvent` indicate that startup work is complete, followed by the accepting-traffic readiness state.

A runner that imports required local data may fit this phase. An unbounded remote call does not: it can delay readiness or make every restart depend on another service. Startup code should be small, observable, and safe to run under the application's deployment model.

sections.title: The useful Spring Boot 3.3.1 startup model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
  A["SpringApplication.run"] --> E["Prepare Environment and active profiles"]
  E --> C["Create and initialize the ApplicationContext"]
  C --> L["Load primary source, components, and auto-configuration"]
  L --> R["Refresh context and create singleton beans"]
  R --> W["Start embedded server for a web application"]
  W --> U["ApplicationRunner and CommandLineRunner"]
  U --> Y["Ready event and accepting-traffic state"]
  R -. startup exception .-> F["Failure report and failed event"]
  U -. startup exception .-> F
```

questions.question: What is Spring Boot Actuator?
questions.title: Spring Boot Actuator for production monitoring
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot Actuator is the production-oriented part of Spring Boot that adds endpoints and instrumentation for observing and managing a running application. After adding `spring-boot-starter-actuator`, features such as health, information, metrics, loggers, mappings, and environment details can be enabled and selectively exposed, secured, and connected to monitoring systems.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Add `spring-boot-starter-actuator` to enable Boot's production-ready monitoring and management features.
The default web base path is `/actuator`; health is available at `/actuator/health`.
In Spring Boot 3.3.1, only the health endpoint is exposed over HTTP and JMX by default.
Enabled, exposed, and authorized are separate decisions; an endpoint must satisfy all applicable controls to be available remotely.
Health reports availability, while metrics report measurements such as request timing, JVM use, or application counters.
Expose only the endpoints that operators need, and secure endpoints that reveal or change sensitive state.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Spring Boot Actuator is the production-oriented part of Spring Boot used to observe and, for selected features, manage a running application. Adding `spring-boot-starter-actuator` contributes endpoints and instrumentation without requiring the team to build basic health and metrics plumbing from the beginning.

An endpoint represents one operational concern. `/actuator/health` reports application health, `info` can publish selected application information, `metrics` lets an operator inspect meter names and values, and endpoints such as `loggers` or `mappings` expose other runtime details. The exact endpoints available depend on the application and its dependencies. Metrics are built on Micrometer, so a registry dependency can export them to a monitoring system such as Prometheus.

Three controls should not be mixed up. An endpoint can be enabled in the application, exposed over HTTP or JMX, and protected by an authorization rule. In Spring Boot 3.3.1, only health is exposed over HTTP and JMX by default. With the default web base path, it appears at `/actuator/health`. Adding an endpoint to the exposure list makes it reachable through that technology; it does not prove that the endpoint is safe to publish.

For example, a platform can call the health endpoint for availability checks while a secured monitoring service collects metrics. Health indicators can combine checks for resources the application depends on, and health groups can give liveness and readiness views. A slow remote dependency should not automatically make liveness fail, because that can cause repeated restarts rather than recovery.

Actuator is not a replacement for application logs, traces, alerts, dashboards, or business monitoring. It supplies trustworthy runtime signals and management surfaces. The production design still decides which signals matter, who may read them, how they are protected, and what action an alert should trigger.

sections.title: Turn application state into safe operational signals
sections.content:
**Endpoints are small operational views**

Actuator registers endpoint definitions independently of their transport. HTTP and JMX are common ways to expose them. Over HTTP, the default base path is `/actuator`, followed by the endpoint ID. The health endpoint is therefore `/actuator/health` unless the base path or mapping is changed.

The built-in set covers different jobs. Health summarizes whether the application and selected dependencies can serve their role. Metrics provides measurements through Micrometer. Info exposes explicitly contributed information. Loggers can inspect and change logging levels, while mappings, beans, environment, configuration properties, and thread or heap data can reveal how the process is running. Not every endpoint should be available to every caller.

**Enabled, exposed, and secured**

An endpoint must be enabled and exposed through the chosen technology before a remote client can use it. Boot 3.3.1 exposes only health over HTTP and JMX by default because operational endpoints can contain sensitive information or allow changes. Exposure settings choose the endpoint IDs; Spring Security, a firewall, or another access layer decides who may call them. If an application defines its own `SecurityFilterChain`, Boot backs off and that application configuration owns the actuator rules.

**Design health for the platform using it**

Liveness answers whether the process should be restarted. Readiness answers whether it should receive traffic. A database outage may make one business operation unavailable and may affect readiness, but placing every external check in liveness can create restart loops. Health groups and carefully chosen indicators let the application describe these different meanings.

Metrics need the same care. A timer or counter becomes useful only when its name, tags, units, and alert threshold are stable. High-cardinality tags such as user IDs create an expensive and noisy metric space. Actuator provides the measurement path; an observability design turns those measurements into useful dashboards and alerts.

sections.title: Choose the signal for the operational question
sections.content:
| Signal or endpoint | Question it answers | Exposure note |
|---|---|---|
| `health` | Can this application or health group perform its role? | Default web endpoint; details should follow an access policy |
| `metrics` | What values and timings is the process recording? | Usually collected by secured monitoring infrastructure |
| `info` | Which selected build or application details were contributed? | Expose only information intended for callers |
| `loggers` | What are the current logging levels, and may they be changed? | A management operation that needs strong access control |
| `env`, `configprops`, `heapdump` | What configuration or runtime data is present? | Potentially sensitive; do not expose broadly |

sections.title: Add Actuator and expose a small endpoint set
sections.content:
```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

```properties
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics
management.endpoint.health.show-details=when-authorized
```

The configuration makes three endpoint IDs available over HTTP; it is not an authorization policy. Add an appropriate network and Spring Security policy before exposing operational data outside a trusted environment.
